name: LGD-2226

lead: LGD-2226 is an oral, nonsteroidal SARM reported in 2006. Users take it hoping to add muscle and a more muscular physique with less prostate stimulation than testosterone.

It binds and activates the androgen receptor. In animals it showed anabolic effects on muscle and bone, with comparatively smaller effects on prostate weight and luteinizing hormone than testosterone. It was researched for muscle wasting and osteoporosis, not cosmetic use. No published human trial was identified.

paras: It is sold online as a research chemical in physique-focused circles, typically alongside training and diet. Reports are anecdotal.
No human safety data exist. SARMs as a class have been linked to liver enzyme elevations and hormone suppression, are banned in sport, and are unapproved by the FDA.

chain: Anabolic effect on muscle and bone
angle.text: LGD-2226 is a SARM that users take hoping to add muscle by activating the androgen receptor, with less prostate stimulation than testosterone. Animal studies showed anabolic effects on muscle and bone.

lead: LGD-2226 is an investigational, orally active, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the quinolinone chemical class, reported in the medicinal chemistry literature in 2006.[1][2] In animal studies it behaved as a potent, selective androgen receptor agonist with anabolic effects on muscle and bone and smaller effects on prostate weight and luteinizing hormone than testosterone.[1]

The appearance link is muscle. SARMs were designed to deliver the muscle- and bone-building effects of androgens while sparing tissues such as the prostate, and the physique-oriented segment of the fitness world discusses compounds of the class as routes to lean mass and a more muscular look.[2][3] LGD-2226 was developed for muscle wasting and osteoporosis rather than for cosmetic purposes.[1]

It is not an approved medicine, SARMs as a class have been on the World Anti-Doping Agency's Prohibited List since 2008, and no published human trial of LGD-2226 was identified.[1][4] Most published work after its discovery concerns how it can be detected in sports and animal doping control.[5][4][6][7]
infobox: SARMs prohibited by WADA since January 2008[1][4]

paras: LGD-2226 is a 6-dialkylamino-4-trifluoromethylquinolin-2(1H)-one carrying two trifluoroethyl groups on the amino nitrogen.[1] Four 6-alkylamino-2-quinolinone model SARMs, including the advanced candidate LGD-2226, were synthesised for a 2007 doping-control screening study that mapped their mass-spectrometric fragmentation.[5]

LGD-2226 is a potent, selective agonist of the androgen receptor.[1] SARMs in general act as agonists in bone and muscle and as partial agonists or antagonists in tissues such as the prostate. The tissue selectivity is still debated: proposals include that SARMs are not converted to a more potent form by 5-alpha-reductase as testosterone is, tissue-specific coregulator expression, and tissue-selective uptake.[2]

A 2007 Endocrinology paper cited by Wikipedia reported oral efficacy of LGD-2226 on bone, muscle and sexual function in animals with reduced impact on the prostate relative to testosterone, and a 2008 Endocrinology study examined cell-specific activation of skeletal alpha-actin by the compound.[1]

In vitro work with equine liver microsomes identified three phase I metabolites of LGD-2226, reported for the first time in a 2022 study of seven non-steroidal SARMs.[6] A 2020 assay for monitoring SARMs in racehorse and cattle blood listed a detection capability of 2 ng/mL for LGD-2226.[7]

The first non-steroidal SARMs were developed independently in 1998 by groups at the University of Tennessee and Ligand Pharmaceuticals, and the term SARM was introduced in 1999.[2] A discovery paper on a quinolinone-based SARM class, including LGD-2226, was published in 2006 in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry.[1]

WADA added SARMs to its Prohibited List in 2008, and a 2007 paper had already described screening methods for 2-quinolinone-derived SARMs including LGD-2226.[1][5][4] Wikipedia notes that the compound was encountered as a designer drug by at least 2020.[1]

As of 2023, neither the FDA nor the European Medicines Agency had approved any SARM.[2] SARMs are sold on gray markets, often labelled as research chemicals not for human consumption, and one study cited by Wikipedia found most online products labelled as SARMs were mislabelled.[2] In Australia SARMs are Schedule 4 (prescription-only).[2] Bodybuilders and athletes use compounds of the class, often at doses above those in trials, and athletes in several leagues have tested positive.[2] LGD-2226 is mentioned in lists of SARMs on forums such as T Nation as a compound that 'affects both muscle and bone', echoing the encyclopedia description.[3][1]

No human safety data specific to LGD-2226 were identified. For the class, Wikipedia reports mild and infrequent adverse events in trials but notes SARMs can raise liver enzymes and lower HDL cholesterol, that several case reports link recreational use to liver injury, and that they can reduce gonadotropins, testosterone and SHBG in a dose- and compound-dependent way, less than testosterone does.[2] Because SARMs cannot be aromatised to oestrogen, they do not cause oestrogenic effects such as gynecomastia; their virilising potential is poorly characterised.[2]

No studies found. The published work on LGD-2226 consists of laboratory and animal pharmacology,[1] and analytical papers on how the compound and its metabolites can be detected in doping-control samples, including equine metabolism studies.[5][4][6][7] For context, trials of other SARMs, chiefly enobosarm (ostarine), involved about 25 studies and over 1,700 people by 2020; a phase III enobosarm trial increased lean body mass without significantly improving physical function.[2]

timeline.event: Ligand Pharmaceuticals and the University of Tennessee independently develop the first non-steroidal SARMs.[2]
Discovery of the compound as a novel SARM is reported (van Oeveren et al.).[1]
Animal study of oral efficacy on bone, muscle and sexual function is published; screening methods for quinolinone SARMs are described.[1][5]
LGD-2226 is encountered as a designer drug.[1]
